samples.text:
In many countries today, people use bank cards and mobile phone apps to pay for things more than cash. In my opinion, this change has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that paying by card or phone is very quick and easy. You only need to touch the card on the machine and the payment is finish in a second. People do not need to carry a lot of coins and notes in their wallet, and they do not need to go to the bank to take out money. Secondly, it is safer. If a person lose his wallet with cash, the money is gone forever, but if he lose his card, he can call the bank and block it. Also, the apps show all the payments, so people can check how much money they spend every month and control their budget.

However, there are some disadvantages as well. Some old people do not know how to use smartphone apps and they prefer to pay with cash, so they may find it difficult in shops which only accept cards. In addition, some people spend more money when they pay by card, because they do not see the money leaving their hands. Another problem is that hackers can steal the information of bank accounts online. Finally, if there is a problem with the internet or electricity, people cannot pay at all.

In conclusion, using cards and mobile apps have some disadvantages, such as problems for elderly people and the risk of online crime. However, I believe that the advantages like speed, convenience and safety are more important, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear judgement · relevant ideas on both sides but briefly developed · mechanical linking and a repetitive conclusion · adequate vocabulary · several verb form and agreement errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In many parts of the world, cash is gradually being replaced by debit cards, contactless payments and mobile phone apps. Although this trend creates difficulties for certain groups, I believe that its advantages are greater than its disadvantages.

The most obvious benefit of digital payments is convenience. Paying with a card or phone takes only a few seconds, there is no need to search for the correct change, and people can shop online or transfer money to friends instantly. This also benefits businesses, which save the time and expense of counting, storing and transporting cash. Secondly, electronic payment is generally safer. Carrying large amounts of cash makes people a target for theft, whereas a lost card can be cancelled immediately. In addition, every digital transaction is recorded, which makes it harder for criminals to avoid paying tax or to hide illegal earnings. Banking apps also allow users to monitor their spending in detail, which can help them manage their finances more responsibly.

Nevertheless, there are some drawbacks to a cashless society. Elderly people and those without bank accounts or smartphones may be excluded if shops and services stop accepting cash. It is often argued that people spend more when they pay digitally, since tapping a card feels less real than handing over notes. There are also concerns about privacy, as banks and technology companies can collect detailed information about where and how people spend their money, and about vulnerability to cyber-attacks or technical failures.

However, these problems can be reduced if governments ensure that cash remains available for those who need it and introduce strong rules on data protection.

In conclusion, although digital payments raise issues of exclusion, overspending and privacy, their speed, safety and transparency make them a positive development. Overall, the advantages clearly outweighs the disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported, with drawbacks acknowledged · logical progression and varied linking · good collocation (contactless payments, cyber-attacks) · frequent error-free sentences, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The steady decline of cash in favour of cards, contactless technology and mobile wallets has been one of the quieter revolutions in everyday life. Although this shift poses genuine risks for certain groups, I am convinced that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages, provided that access to cash is not abolished altogether.

For consumers, the appeal of digital payments lies chiefly in their convenience. Transactions are completed in seconds, purchases can be made online or across borders without exchanging currency, and money can be sent to friends or family at the touch of a button. Electronic payments also offer greater security for individuals: a stolen wallet full of notes is usually lost for good, whereas a card can be frozen instantly and fraudulent transactions are often refunded. At a wider level, a largely cashless economy is more transparent. Because every payment leaves a record, it becomes considerably harder to conceal income from tax authorities or to launder the proceeds of crime, which ultimately benefits honest taxpayers. Businesses, meanwhile, save on the costs of handling, securing and banking physical money.

The drawbacks, however, should not be underestimated. Those who are elderly, on low incomes or living in areas with poor connectivity may find themselves excluded from essential services if cash ceases to be accepted. Digital payments can also make spending feel less tangible, which may encourage some people to overspend or fall into debt. Furthermore, a society dependent on electronic systems is exposed to cyber-attacks and outages, and the detailed data generated by every transaction raises legitimate questions about surveillance and privacy.

These concerns, though serious, argue for safeguards rather than a rejection of digital payments. Guaranteeing that cash remains legal tender and widely accepted, while enforcing robust data-protection standards, would address the most significant risks.

In conclusion, the move away from cash brings efficiency, security and transparency that benefit individuals and society as a whole. As long as vulnerable groups are protected, the advantages of this trend clearly outweigh its disadvantages.
samples.why: Clear, qualified judgement sustained throughout · ideas well developed at individual and societal level · skilful cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (legal tender, launder the proceeds) · wide range of error-free structures.
